groups.passage:
Learning from a Mistake

At a furniture workshop, apprentices used to receive a score at the end of each week. A score told them whether their work met the expected standard, but it did not always show them what to improve. The workshop introduced a short feedback session after each practical task. Instead of simply pointing out errors, the instructor asked each apprentice to identify one aspect of the work that had gone well and one that needed improvement.

At first, apprentices often gave vague answers such as 'I need to work faster'. The instructor encouraged them to describe a specific action: for example, checking the alignment of two pieces before applying glue. Each apprentice then chose a target for the following task.

After several weeks, the instructor noticed that apprentices were asking for help earlier in the process. She continued to assess the finished products, but she also collected notes about the apprentices' targets. These notes helped her recognise difficulties that were shared by several members of the group and plan a demonstration accordingly.

questions.question_text: What limitation did the weekly scores have?

options.text: They were based only on attendance.
They were given before practical work began.
They measured speed instead of finished quality.
They did not always show apprentices how to improve.

questions.question_text: What did the instructor ask apprentices to identify after a task?

options.text: The total cost of the materials.
One strength and one area for improvement.
Two mistakes made by other apprentices.
The number of tasks completed that week.

questions.question_text: Why does the passage mention checking alignment before applying glue?

options.text: It illustrates a specific action an apprentice can improve.
It describes the grading system for finished furniture.
It explains why the workshop stopped using glue.
It identifies the only difficulty shared by all apprentices.

questions.question_text: Which change in behaviour did the instructor notice?

options.text: Apprentices asked for weekly scores only.

questions.question_text: How did the individual notes help the instructor plan teaching?

options.text: They showed which apprentices should leave the programme.
They determined how much furniture each person could sell.
They revealed recurring difficulties across the group.
They allowed her to stop assessing products.

questions.question_text: What is the passage mainly about?

options.text: Replacing all practical training with written examinations.
Teaching apprentices to work without any guidance.
Increasing the furniture workshop's weekly output.
Using specific feedback to support practical learning.

groups.passage:
Preparing a Community Hall for Floods

A community hall near a river was closed for four months after floodwater damaged its floor, electrical equipment and storage cupboards. When the hall was repaired, the committee considered moving the building. However, suitable land was expensive, and the existing hall was close to the bus station. The committee decided to reduce the damage that a future flood might cause.

An engineer recommended moving electrical sockets higher up the walls and replacing the wooden cupboards in the ground-floor rooms with washable units. Portable furniture could be moved to an upper storage room when a flood warning was issued. The committee prepared a checklist specifying who would move each item and where it should go.

A practice exercise revealed that some large tables could not fit through the staircase door. The committee replaced those tables with folding ones. It also reviewed its insurance policy and agreed to cancel events whenever an official flood warning was issued. The building remained vulnerable to flooding, but the committee hoped that the measures would shorten the period needed to reopen after the water receded.

questions.question_text: Why did the committee decide against relocating the hall?

options.text: Suitable land was expensive, and the current location was convenient.
The engineer guaranteed the river would never flood again.
The hall had suffered no damage to electrical equipment.
The bus station was due to move to another district.

questions.question_text: Which modification did the engineer recommend?

options.text: Building a new bus station beside the hall.
Installing wooden cupboards on the ground floor.

questions.question_text: What was the purpose of the checklist?

options.text: To calculate the engineer's hourly fee.
To assign responsibilities and destinations for moved items.
To list events that had taken place before the flood.
To record the price of land near the river.

questions.question_text: What problem was discovered in the practice exercise?

options.text: The storage room was completely empty.
The washable cupboards could not be cleaned.
The new sockets were placed below the old ones.
Some tables were too large for the staircase door.

questions.question_text: The word receded in the final sentence is closest in meaning to -------.
What does the passage suggest is the realistic aim of the improvements?

options.text: To reduce losses and make recovery quicker after flooding.
To prevent the river from overflowing anywhere nearby.
To keep the hall open throughout every flood warning.
To remove the need for insurance permanently.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
Measuring Changes in Starlight

Some stars appear to become brighter and fainter over periods ranging from hours to months. To study these changes, astronomers need measurements made at different times. A small university invited amateur observers to help collect data on a star whose brightness varied over several weeks. The amateurs owned different cameras, so the university needed a method that allowed observations from different equipment to be compared.

The researchers asked participants to photograph the target star together with two nearby stars known to have stable brightness. Instead of recording only the amount of light detected from the target, participants calculated how bright it appeared relative to the comparison stars. This helped reduce differences caused by camera settings or by a thin layer of cloud affecting the whole image. However, photographs in which the stars were too faint to measure reliably were excluded.

The observation schedule also mattered. Most volunteers lived in the same country and could not observe the target during daylight hours. To reduce gaps in the record, the university recruited additional volunteers in other parts of the world. Participants recorded the time of each photograph using a shared time standard, allowing data collected in different time zones to be arranged correctly.

After several months, the resulting measurements showed a regular pattern of increasing and decreasing brightness. The researchers compared the pattern with previously collected measurements before drawing conclusions about its period. They stressed that participation alone could not guarantee useful data. Consistent observation procedures, accurate time records and checks on image quality were all essential to turning contributions from many individuals into a reliable scientific record.

questions.question_text: Why did the university recruit amateur observers?

options.text: To determine the distance between the comparison stars.
To manufacture identical cameras for the university.
To collect measurements of the star at different times.

questions.question_text: Why were two nearby stable stars included in each image?

options.text: They provided reference points for comparing the target's brightness.
They showed how quickly the target moved across the sky.
They identified the model of camera used by the volunteer.
They enabled the observers to remove clouds from photographs.

questions.question_text: Which photographs were excluded from the measurements?

options.text: Those taken by volunteers outside the university's country.
Those showing both comparison stars clearly.
Those in which the stars were too faint to measure reliably.
Those taken with different camera models.

questions.question_text: What does This refer to in This helped reduce differences caused by camera settings?

options.text: Recording only the target's detected light.
Excluding all photographs taken in daylight.
Calculating brightness relative to the comparison stars.

questions.question_text: Why did the university recruit volunteers in other regions of the world?

options.text: To ensure all photographs were taken at the same local hour.
To replace the stable stars with different comparison stars.
To reduce time gaps when the original observers could not see the star.
To measure differences between university and amateur cameras only.

questions.question_text: Why was a shared time standard important?

options.text: It ensured that every volunteer saw exactly the same sky conditions.
It meant that images no longer needed quality checks.
It made the target star vary at a regular rate.
It allowed observations from different time zones to be put in correct order.

questions.question_text: What did the researchers do before drawing conclusions about the period of variation?

options.text: They removed all measurements gathered by amateurs.
They assumed the period was exactly one month.
They repeated every photograph with a single camera.
They compared the new pattern with earlier measurements.

questions.question_text: Which statement best expresses the author's central argument?

options.text: A large number of photographs automatically guarantees accurate measurements.
The main difficulty in astronomy is persuading volunteers to buy equipment.
Only identical professional cameras can measure variable stars.
Many observers can produce reliable scientific data if their methods and records are consistent.
